passage: Every Thursday at seven, Nkechi set up the moth trap in the university garden in Manchester: same corner, same white sheet, same flask of rooibos. When a girl from her building, Hana, wandered over and said, "Cool light," Nkechi answered, "It's a special lamp for moths, and please don't stand on the sheet." Hana stepped back, laughing. "Fair. What have you caught?" Nkechi talked for twenty minutes about the elephant hawk-moth: its pink wings, the way its caterpillar pretends to be a snake. Hana didn't seem to mind the lecture. The next Thursday she arrived at seven exactly, with her own flask and a sketch. "I drew the hawk-moth." Nkechi studied it. "The antennae are wrong. The rest is good." Hana grinned. "Then show me."

qa.q: What did Nkechi drink at the moth trap every Thursday?
qa.a: A flask of rooibos.

qa.q: What does Hana arriving at seven exactly suggest about how she feels?
qa.a: It suggests she enjoyed Nkechi's company and the moths, and wants to share the interest and respect the routine.

qa.q: Which choice by Hana turned a blunt answer into a friendship?
qa.a: Hana laughed and asked a question instead of taking offence, then came back with her own sketch.

qa.q: How might another student see Nkechi's comment about the antennae?
qa.a: Someone else might find it rude, but Hana sees it as honest help and a way to learn more.

grounding: It shows a young adult with a deep passion, direct speech and a steady routine, whose honesty and focus draw in Hana, who comes to share the interest.

passage: The hostel common room was loud with the TV, so Lakshmi read in the stairwell, as she did every night from nine to ten, headphones on, a photocopy of a temple inscription on her knees. Rajni from Room 14 sat two steps below with her history assignment. "You're the inscriptions person, right? Could you check this?" Lakshmi read it once. "Your second paragraph is wrong. That grant is Chola, not Pallava. The rest is fine." Rajni blinked, then laughed. "Okay, blunt. Thank you." "I'm not being rude. You asked." "I know. It's actually useful." Lakshmi showed her how to spot the older letter shapes, and the hour vanished. At ten sharp, Lakshmi stood up. "Same time tomorrow? Quiet only." "Quiet only," Rajni agreed.

qa.q: Where does Lakshmi read every night from nine to ten?
qa.a: In the stairwell, because the common room is loud with the TV.

qa.q: Why does Lakshmi add, 'I'm not being rude. You asked'?
qa.a: She seems to worry her direct answer might be taken badly and wants Rajni to know she meant it as honest help.

qa.q: What made this conversation grow into a friendship?
qa.a: Rajni accepted the blunt feedback as useful, and they bonded over the inscriptions while keeping Lakshmi's quiet routine.

qa.q: How does Rajni see Lakshmi's directness by the end of the evening?
qa.a: Rajni sees it as useful and honest, and happily agrees to Lakshmi's quiet-only rule.

grounding: It shows a young adult with a deep interest, direct speech and a need for quiet and routine, whose honesty helps a new friendship form.

"Irawati, your slides were too long. Nobody reads eleven bullet points."
Irawati blinked. "Wow. Okay, Sonali."
"It's true. The birds part was good, though. The part about the barbet nest."
Irawati laughed despite herself. "You're the only one who noticed the birds."
"I've logged forty-three species on campus. I walk at six every morning, same route." Sonali pulled out a worn notebook. "Here. Barbet, coppersmith, the paradise flycatcher by the library."
"Can I come tomorrow?"
"Six sharp. We don't talk near the pond."
"Fine. Six sharp."
Next morning Irawati was at the gate at five-fifty-five.

qa.q: How many species has Sonali logged on campus?
qa.a: Sonali has logged forty-three species on campus.

qa.q: How did Irawati feel when Sonali criticised her slides?
qa.a: She was a bit stung and surprised at first, then amused and curious once Sonali praised the birds part.

qa.q: What made the friendship start well despite the blunt comment?
qa.a: Irawati looked past the direct words and joined Sonali's passion, accepting her routine of six sharp and silence near the pond.

qa.q: How might Sonali see Irawati turning up at five-fifty-five?
qa.a: Sonali would likely feel pleased and respected, since Irawati honoured the six-sharp routine and shared the love of birds.

grounding: Shows a young adult with a deep passion, direct speech and a need for routine and quiet, whose honesty and focus help a friendship form around a shared interest.

passage: In my first year of college I fixed old radios in my hostel room every evening, seven to ten, headphones on. People called me strange. Once, in the canteen, I told Urmila her theory about signal noise was wrong, and she stared at me before walking off. I felt terrible for days; I had only been being honest. A week later she knocked on my door holding a broken valve radio. "Fine, Jeevan. Prove it." We spent four hours on it. It crackled into life at midnight, playing old film songs. Now the radio club meets in my room, and Urmila tells new members, "Jeevan will tell you the truth, and he'll be right." I still keep my evenings quiet.

qa.q: What did Urmila bring to Jeevan's door?
qa.a: She brought a broken valve radio.

qa.q: How did Jeevan feel after the canteen moment with Urmila?
qa.a: Jeevan felt terrible and confused for days, having meant only to be honest, not to hurt her.

qa.q: What helped Jeevan's honesty become a strength in friendship?
qa.a: Sharing the work on the radio with Urmila showed Jeevan's focus and skill, so Jeevan's directness became something people trusted.

qa.q: How does Urmila now see Jeevan's honest style?
qa.a: Urmila sees it as reliable; she tells new members Jeevan will tell them the truth and be right.

grounding: Shows a young adult with a deep passion, direct speech and a need for routine and quiet, whose honesty and focus draw a friend through a shared interest.

passage:
Lab supervisor's note, summer interns, week six.
Harsha, 20, has spent every free hour on the ant colony study, arriving at 8:00 and leaving at 5:00 exactly. The intern desk by the printer was too noisy, so we moved Harsha to the corner bench, and the counts improved immediately. In Tuesday's meeting Harsha said my protocol "wastes two days." It was blunt, and it was correct; we changed it. Ishita, the other intern, was hurt by a similar comment at first, but now the two of them eat lunch by the colony tanks talking about queens and tunnels. Next step: ask Harsha to present the method change at the department seminar.

qa.q: Where did the supervisor move Harsha, and what happened?
qa.a: Harsha was moved to the corner bench, and the counts improved immediately.

qa.q: How did Ishita feel after Harsha's blunt comment at first, and later?
qa.a: Ishita was hurt at first, but later seemed comfortable and friendly, eating lunch with Harsha and talking about ants.

qa.q: How did the supervisor handle Harsha's direct feedback, and why was that wise?
qa.a: The supervisor took the blunt point seriously, checked it, changed the protocol and planned to let Harsha present it.

qa.q: What would change if the supervisor had kept Harsha at the noisy desk?
qa.a: Harsha's work would likely have suffered, and the lab might have missed the focus that made the counts better.

grounding: Shows a young adult whose deep interest, honest speech and need for quiet routine bring real strengths and a friendship built on a shared passion.

passage:
14 Nov
Woke at 6:10. Tea, oats, same as always. The hostel was quiet, which is my favourite time.
Spent four hours in the library on moths. Did you know some moths navigate by the moon? I did not stop to eat. I forgot.
In the seminar, Rohan asked what I thought of his presentation. I said the second half didn't follow from the data. His face went stiff. I meant it as help. I need to remember people sometimes want a softer first sentence.
But then, at the nature club, a girl called Charu showed me her photo of a luna moth. We talked for an hour straight. She said, "Finally, someone who doesn't get bored." Same time next Friday.
Good day. Tired now. Earplugs in.
Sudha

qa.q: What time did Sudha wake up?
How did Sudha feel after the talk with Charu?
qa.a: Sudha felt happy and excited, having finally found someone who shared the same deep interest in moths.

qa.q: What could Sudha try next time someone asks for honest feedback?
qa.a: Keep the honest point but start with a softer first sentence, so the helpful meaning comes across.

qa.q: How might Rohan have felt about Sudha's comment?
qa.a: He probably felt stung and a bit embarrassed, even though the comment was honest and meant as help.

grounding: Sudha's deep passion, direct speech and need for routine and quiet show strengths of focus and honesty, and a friendship forms around a shared interest.
